title: Background responses and durable agents
summary: Four different things get called long-running: provider background responses (a continuation token you poll), background agents (delegated child tasks), workflow checkpoints, and the Durable Extension (durable sessions and orchestrations that wait without compute).
useIf: A request outlives one HTTP call, a stream may break, a human may take hours, or work must survive a restart and scale across workers.
avoidIf: Runs finish in seconds and a retry is cheap: the extra mechanisms add state, storage and operational cost.

explain.md: **Background responses.** Ask a provider to run a request in the background. The first call may finish at once (no token) or return a **continuation token**. Poll by passing the token back, or resume an interrupted stream with the token from the last update. A null token means done, failed, or unable to proceed (for example it needs user input). C#: `AllowBackgroundResponses = true` in `AgentRunOptions`; Python: `options={'background': True}`. Only agents on the OpenAI Responses API qualify in .NET (OpenAI and Azure OpenAI Responses); in Python the OpenAI Responses, Azure OpenAI Responses or Foundry clients qualify, and with `FoundryChatClient` you keep the same session while polling so local tool loops can continue [[tr28]].

**Background agents** are different and experimental: a parent agent delegates tasks to named child agents with six tools (`background_agents_start_task`, `_wait_for_first_completion`, `_get_task_results`, `_get_all_tasks`, `_continue_task`, `_clear_completed_task`). Status is `running`, `completed`, `failed` or `lost`. There is **no cancel tool**, in-flight work does not survive a restart (it becomes `lost`) and child approvals are not proxied to the parent [[tr29]].

**Durable Extension** (Beta in Python, preview in .NET, checked 2026-10-13). Two hosting models: **Azure Functions** or **bring your own compute** (containers, Kubernetes, workers), backed by Durable Task (Durable Task Scheduler recommended). It persists sessions, checkpoints graph workflows, resumes after failure, pauses for human input or events **without using compute or tokens**, streams reliably through a broker such as Redis, and cleans idle sessions with a session TTL. Flex Consumption can scale to thousands of instances or to zero. Inside orchestrations call agents through `context.GetAgent()` (.NET) or `app.get_agent(context, name)` (Python) so calls are replay-safe [[tr30]].

blocks.title: Poll a background response
Durable agents on Azure Functions
Poll a background response
blocks.code:
session = agent.create_session()
response = await agent.run(messages='Write a very long report.', session=session,
                           options={'background': True})
while response.continuation_token is not None:
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    response = await agent.run(session=session,
        options={'continuation_token': response.continuation_token})
print(response.text)

blocks.title: Durable agents on Azure Functions

whereToUse: Long reasoning requests where a browser call would time out: background responses
Streaming UIs that must reconnect after a drop: resume with the last continuation token
Approval flows that wait hours or days with no idle compute: Durable Extension
Agents that must keep conversations across process crashes and scale-out
MCP exposure of agents from Azure Functions via the MCP server trigger

use: The request may exceed client or gateway timeouts
A person or event gates progress for hours or days
Workers are stateless and any worker must resume any run
avoid: Short, cheap runs: a simple retry is enough
You need cancellation of background-agent tasks: the provider has no cancel tool
Pre-release packages are banned and you cannot take the Beta or preview Durable packages
Assuming background responses work with every provider: support is provider-specific
flips: Waits are long and compute costs matter: use durable orchestrations with external events and timers
You only need to resume a graph in your own process: standard checkpoint storage may be enough

pitfalls.symptom: Polling never ends or returns an empty response
pitfalls.cause: The token went null because the run needs user input or failed; null does not always mean success
pitfalls.fix: Check status, errors and user-input content, then continue with a new run

pitfalls.symptom: Background child tasks show `lost` after a deploy
pitfalls.cause: In-process task handles and child sessions do not survive restarts
pitfalls.fix: Use durable orchestration or workflow checkpoints for work that must survive

pitfalls.symptom: An orchestration replays and calls the model twice
pitfalls.cause: The agent was invoked outside `context.GetAgent()` or `app.get_agent()`, so the call is not replay-safe
pitfalls.fix: Call agents inside orchestrations only through the durable agent handle

scenarios.title: Reports that take ten minutes
scenarios.situation: A reasoning model takes up to 10 minutes per report. The web gateway times out at 60 seconds. Users should see progress and survive page refreshes. Volume is 500 reports a day.
unknowns: Do local tools need to run during the report?
Is the provider on the supported list?
scenarios.question: What mechanism do you use?

options.name: Background responses: start with the background option, store the continuation token with the session, and poll or resume the stream from the web tier
options.why: The provider runs the work, the token survives refreshes, and no custom orchestration is needed.
options.tradeoff: Provider-specific, and you must store tokens and sessions safely.

options.name: Increase gateway timeouts to 15 minutes
options.why: Fragile and holds connections; any network blip loses the run.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable for internal tools on stable networks.

options.name: Durable orchestration for every report
options.tradeoff: Heavier than needed for one provider call, on Beta or preview packages.

flips.if: Reports include human review steps lasting hours
flips.then: Use durable orchestrations with external events.

flips.if: The provider does not support background responses
flips.then: Run the call in a worker and persist the result yourself.

scenarios.takeaway: A single long provider call calls for a continuation token, not an orchestration.

scenarios.title: Contract approvals lasting days
scenarios.situation: An agent drafts contract clauses, a lawyer approves within 1 to 5 days, then the agent files the result. 200 contracts a month. Compute cost while waiting must be near zero.
unknowns: Can the team adopt Beta or preview packages?
What if the lawyer never answers?
scenarios.question: What do you build on?

options.name: Durable Extension on Azure Functions: orchestration with `wait_for_external_event`, a 5-day timer for escalation, session TTL cleanup
options.why: Waits consume no compute or tokens, scale to zero, and the orchestration resumes with full context.
options.tradeoff: Beta (Python) or preview (.NET) packages and the Durable programming model.

options.name: Workflow with a request port and Cosmos DB checkpoints on your own container host
options.why: Stable core and durable pending requests.
options.tradeoff: You keep a host running or restart it on demand, and wire timers and wake-ups yourself.

options.name: A background agent that sleeps until approval
options.why: Holds compute and loses state on restart (status `lost`).
options.tradeoff: Fine for minutes, never for days.

flips.then: Use the stable workflow checkpoint approach with your own timer and trigger.

flips.if: Approval arrives within the same session
flips.then: A tool approval with a persisted session is simpler.

scenarios.takeaway: Days-long waits are a durable-runtime problem, not a prompt problem.

quiz.q: After a service restart, background-agent tasks report `lost`. What happened?
options: In-process task handles and child sessions did not survive the restart
The Durable Task Scheduler purged them
quiz.explain: The docs say a task becomes lost when its in-process handle or child session is unavailable, such as after a restart or session restore. Only metadata remains.

quiz.q: Which statements about background responses are correct? Select all.
options: A null continuation token can mean done, failed or waiting for user input
They are enabled with `AllowBackgroundResponses` (.NET) or `options={'background': True}` (Python)
They work with every agent type
A broken stream can be resumed with the last update's token
quiz.explain: Support depends on the provider (OpenAI and Azure OpenAI Responses, plus Foundry in Python), not every agent type.

quiz.q: You need approvals that may wait five days, scale-to-zero cost while waiting and recovery after a crash. Which option is the best fit?
options: The Durable Extension with an external-event wait
quiz.explain: Durable orchestrations wait without compute and resume with context. Background responses cover one provider call, and background agents lose work on restart.

flashcards.front: What does a null continuation token mean?
flashcards.back: The background operation is complete, failed, or cannot proceed (for example it needs user input).
Responses: one provider request you poll or resume with a token. Agents: a parent delegates tasks to child agents; experimental, no cancel tool, lost on restart.

flashcards.front: Name two Durable Extension hosting models.
flashcards.back: Azure Functions (serverless, scale to zero) and bring-your-own compute (containers, Kubernetes, workers) on Durable Task.
